blocks.text: A pH curve is a graph of the pH of the solution verses the volume of titrant added.

blocks.title: Equivalence point
blocks.text: The equivalence point is the point at which the amount of titrant added is just enough to neutralize the analyte solution completely.

Titration curves show how the pH of an acidic or basic solution changes as a basic or acidic solution is added to it. We can use the titration curve to choose an indicator that will show when the titration is complete and we reach the equivalence point. The end point of the titration occurs when the indicator changes color. We choose an indicator with an end point close to the equivalence point.

As an example of a strong acid–strong base titration, let’s consider the titration of HCl with NaOH. Initially, the solution contains only the strong acid. Since the acid is strong, it completely dissociates, leading to a high concentration of H⁺ ions and the pH is very low.
As NaOH is added, OH⁻ ions from NaOH begin to neutralize the H⁺ ions from HCl and pH of the solution rises.

The equivalence point is reached when the amount of OH⁻ added is stoichiometrically equal to the amount of H⁺ originally present in the acid. The pH at the equivalence point in a strong acid-strong base titration is 7.0. The titration curve at this stage shows a steep rise in pH, changing quickly from acidic to neutral. The pH value at the endpoint changes about from 4.0 to 10.0. These titrations have a pH of 7.0 at equivalence, so, such phenolphthalein as indicator can be used as they show different colours in this range.

blocks.alt: Titration curve: pH (0 to 14) against volume of strong base added (0 to 80 mL), with plotted points. The pH starts near 1, rises slowly, jumps almost vertically at 40 mL and levels off near 12.5. A dashed line marks pH = 7.00 at equivalence point. Coloured bands on the steep part show phenolphthalein (about pH 8.2 to 10) and methyl red (about pH 4.4 to 6.2), each labelled beside a flask.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.3: Strong acid-strong base titration curve (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.3).

blocks.text: Consider the titration of aqueous NH₃ with HCl. Initially, the solution contains only the weak base and it only partially dissociates, with a lower concentration of OH⁻ ions compared to a strong base. The initial pH will be greater than 7 but lower than the pH of a strong base. As HCl is added, the concentration of OH⁻ decreases, causing a further decrease in pH.

Before reaching the equivalence point, the solution is in a buffer-like region where the pH changes more gradually. The presence of the weak base and its conjugate acid (from the salt formed) creates a buffering effect, which helps to moderate the pH change as the base is added.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Here HCl is added to the weak base, so the buffering moderates the pH change as the acid is added.

blocks.alt: Titration curve: pH (0 to 14) against volume of HCl(aq) added (0 to 80 mL). The pH starts near 11, falls slowly through a buffer region (a pink band along the curve, also the phenolphthalein range), drops steeply at 40 mL and levels off near 1.5. Dashed lines mark about pH 9.2 and pH = 5.27 at equivalence point. A methyl red band crosses the steep drop, labelled beside a flask.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.4: strong acid-weak base titration curve (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.4).

blocks.text: The pH at the equivalence point will be less than 7 (pH = 5.27) because the conjugate acid slightly dissociates, releasing H⁺ ions making the solution acidic (NH₄⁺ → NH₃ + H⁺).

After the equivalence point, the pH of the solution decreases rapidly. This is because the strong acid dissociates completely in water, providing a high concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺), which significantly lowers the pH. Methyl orange has its colour change in this range, therefore, it can be used as an indicator for strong acid-weak base titrations.
